title: In-Context / Few-Shot Learning
oneLineScope: GPT-3 and few-shot prompting: how to specify a task purely in the prompt — no weight updates, no gradient steps — and have a large frozen model perform it.
prose:
Every model we have examined up to this point has been trained on a task by adjusting its weights. Feed the model labeled examples, compute a loss, back-propagate, repeat. When the task changes, the weights change: you fine-tune on sentiment data, then fine-tune again on translation data, and so on. This is the paradigm GPT-1 and BERT both inhabit, despite their very different pretraining objectives. Brown et al. (2020) asked a different question: what if the model is already large enough that you can just tell it what to do, inside the ordinary text that constitutes its input, and it performs the task without a single gradient update? That capability — now called in-context learning — is the headline result of GPT-3, and it changed how the field thought about what a language model is for.

What the prompt is doing

The idea is simplest at the extremes. In zero-shot prompting, the input to the model is just a natural-language instruction — "Translate English to French: 'the cat sat on the mat' →" — with no worked examples at all. The model must infer the task entirely from the instruction. In one-shot prompting, a single input–output demonstration precedes the instruction, giving the model a concrete instance of the format and the mapping expected. In few-shot prompting, \(K\) such demonstrations appear — typically \(K \in \{8, 16, 32\}\), bounded by the model's context window — before the query the model is asked to complete.

A few-shot prompt has a fixed skeleton:

Instruction: [task description in natural language]

Input: [example input 1]  Output: [example output 1]
Input: [example input 2]  Output: [example output 2]
       ... (K times) ...
Input: [query input]       Output:

The model's completion of that final line is the prediction. The weights are frozen throughout — the model's parameters \(\theta\) do not change. Whatever adaptation is happening to the task occurs entirely within the forward pass, as the transformer's attention layers process the full context and the final token's distribution conditions on everything that preceded it.

The mechanics: how can a frozen model "learn" from examples?

This is the question the paper raises honestly and does not fully answer — and it is worth dwelling on, because the word "learning" here is being used loosely. No parameters are updated. The model does not become a sentiment classifier; it generates the most probable continuation of the prompt, and if the prompt is structured so that a sentiment label is the natural next token, then the model produces one. The in-context examples constrain and shape the probability distribution over completions: they establish the output vocabulary ("Positive" or "Negative" rather than any token), they disambiguate the task, and they correct systematic biases in formatting or phrasing. Whether this constitutes learning in any meaningful sense is contested — some researchers prefer the term in-context conditioning — and mechanistic explanations remain an active research area. The prose here tracks what is established; the mechanistic account is open.

What is established: the capability is real, it is measurable, and it scales with model size in ways that smaller models do not exhibit.

GPT-3 at 175 billion parameters

GPT-3 is an autoregressive decoder-only transformer — the architecture of the autoregressive-lm node — trained on roughly 300 billion tokens drawn from filtered CommonCrawl, WebText2, Books1, Books2, and English Wikipedia. Its 175B parameters made it the largest language model publicly reported at the time of publication. The key hyperparameters: \(d_{\text{model}} = 12{,}288\), \(h = 96\) attention heads, \(L = 96\) layers, context window of 2,048 tokens. Training used the ordinary causal language-model objective

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{t} \log P_{\theta}(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1}) \]

where \(\theta\) are the parameters, \(x_1, \ldots, x_T\) are the tokens of a document, and the sum runs over positions \(t\). There is nothing novel in the training procedure; the novelty is scale and what emerged from it.

What GPT-3 could do in context

Brown et al. evaluated GPT-3 on a wide range of tasks — translation, question answering, reading comprehension, arithmetic, commonsense reasoning, Winograd schemas — using only prompt engineering, without any gradient steps. A few results worth anchoring to:

  • On the SuperGLUE benchmark, GPT-3's few-shot performance approached fine-tuned BERT-large on several subtasks, without touching the model's weights. On others it fell short; the results were uneven, not uniformly triumphant.
  • On translation from English to French/German/Romanian, GPT-3 few-shot was competitive with supervised models trained specifically on those language pairs.
  • On arithmetic (three-digit addition, subtraction, multiplication), few-shot performance was surprisingly strong, though it degraded as the number of digits grew.

The paper's §3.3 establishes the scaling relationship directly: zero-shot performance improves modestly from 1B to 175B parameters, but the gap between zero-shot and few-shot widens sharply as the model grows. Small models (1B) show negligible benefit from in-context examples; the GPT-3-scale model exploits them aggressively. This is the connection to the scaling-laws node: in-context ability is not a fixed property of the architecture; it is something that emerges — and strengthens — as scale increases.

The honest accounting of limitations

Brown et al. are candid about several problems. First, prompt sensitivity: the order of the few-shot examples, the exact phrasing of the instruction, and even the formatting of the separator between examples can substantially change performance — sometimes by more than ten percentage points on a task. This sensitivity is not merely a curiosity; it means that reported results depend on choices that are hard to justify systematically, and that GPT-3's "performance" on a benchmark is better understood as performance under a particular prompt design rather than as a fixed capability score. Second, calibration: GPT-3 is often confidently wrong, and its probability estimates do not reliably track correctness. Third, the model repeats itself and can degenerate on long outputs. These are acknowledged limitations, not apologetics retrofitted after the fact.

The deeper conceptual issue: because no gradient computation occurs, in-context learning is sensitive to what is already in the weights — the model can only use the in-context examples to steer toward behaviors that the pretraining distribution made probable. If a mapping is truly foreign to the pretraining corpus, a few in-context examples will not install it. The model is not a blank slate that learns from demonstration; it is a heavily pretrained distribution that conditions on context.

Contrast with fine-tuning

Fine-tuning, in the GPT-1/BERT sense, updates \(\theta\): you continue training on the task data with a cross-entropy loss, the weights shift to encode the task structure, and the model's behavior is permanently altered for that task (on that set of weights). Fine-tuning tends to outperform few-shot prompting on individual tasks where sufficient labeled data exist, particularly for structured-output tasks. But it requires labeled data, a training run, and a separate model checkpoint per task — three costs that scale poorly when the number of tasks is large or the compute budget is limited. In-context learning amortizes those costs: one set of weights, specified by the prompt at inference time. The tradeoff is real in both directions.

Where the story goes next

In-context learning showed that a large pretrained base model is not merely a text predictor — it is a highly general-purpose conditional distribution that can be steered by natural language. The next question the field asked was: can we make that steering more reliable by training the model to follow instructions, rather than hoping it will infer the task from the prompt? That question is what supervised fine-tuning addresses: taking the base model and continuing its training on curated instruction–response pairs, turning a text predictor into an instruction follower.

diagrams.caption: Few-shot prompting feeds a frozen model an instruction, K input–output example pairs, then a query; the model completes the final output without any weight update. Contrasted with fine-tuning, where the model's weights are updated by gradient descent on labeled task data.

An arrow exits to a completion box. Right panel labeled 'Fine-tuning (for contrast)': a task dataset box containing instruction–response pairs feeds via a gradient-update arrow into a base model box, which leads to a fine-tuned model box labeled θ′ with 'weights θ modified' noted. The two panels are separated by a vertical dashed line with 'vs.' in the middle.
diagrams.prompt: Structural comparison diagram split left and right by a vertical dashed divider labeled 'vs.' in the middle. Left side, titled 'In-context / few-shot learning': a tall vertically-oriented prompt box (outlined in blue) containing, from top to bottom: a row labeled 'instruction', then three rows each with an 'input N' box and an 'output N' box connected by a right-arrow (the output boxes in green), a small annotation 'K = 3 examples', and finally a row with a 'query' box (blue) pointing to a dashed empty '?' box. An arrow leads rightward from the prompt box into a 'model (frozen)' box; annotate the model with 'weights θ unchanged'. An arrow exits the model to a small 'completion' box (green). Right side, titled 'Fine-tuning (for contrast)': a 'Task dataset' box containing two instruction→response pair rows feeds downward via an arrow labeled 'gradient update (∂𝓛/∂θ)' into a 'base model + training step' box (outlined in red); an arrow exits right to a 'fine-tuned model (θ′)' box (green, stroke-width thicker), annotated 'weights θ modified'. Bottom annotations: left side 'Forward pass only — no weight changes'; right side 'Weights updated by cross-entropy loss'. Label every element; K = 3 shown explicitly.

diagrams.caption: Accuracy on a representative task rises with the number of in-context examples, and the benefit scales sharply with model size. Small models show negligible gain; large models (GPT-3 scale) show steep improvement. The zero-shot baseline is marked at K = 0.
diagrams.altText: A schematic line chart. Horizontal axis: number of in-context examples K, from 0 (zero-shot) through 1 (one-shot) to few (3–5) and many (10+). Vertical axis: task accuracy. Three curves: a nearly flat grey curve labeled 'small model (little benefit)', a moderately rising blue curve labeled 'medium model', and a steeply rising green curve labeled 'large model (e.g. GPT-3 175B)'. A vertical dashed line at K = 0 is labeled 'zero-shot'. An annotation box reads: 'Few-shot gap widens with scale — a pattern that emerged sharply around 100B+ parameters (Brown et al. 2020, §3.3; emergent is debated — see prose)'.

bibliography.citation: Brown, T., et al. (2020). "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners." NeurIPS 33.
bibliography.annotation: The GPT-3 paper. §1 introduces the zero/one/few-shot taxonomy and the core claim. §3 reports the task evaluations with the scaling breakdown. §3.3 specifically shows the few-shot gap widening with model scale. Appendix G gives the full list of evaluation prompts and is instructive for understanding prompt sensitivity. Read §1 and §3 for the core; §4 for the honest discussion of limitations.

bibliography.citation: Bommasani, R., et al. (2021). "On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models." Stanford CRFM.
bibliography.annotation: A broad survey covering in-context learning in §4.1 with clear conceptual framing. Not a deep technical reference, but situates GPT-3-style prompting in the landscape of what changed in 2020–21. Useful for the reader who wants the wider context before diving into the original paper. Appropriately candid about what is and is not understood mechanistically.

bibliography.citation: Min, S., et al. (2022). "Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations for In-Context Learning." EMNLP.
bibliography.annotation: A careful ablation study showing that the labels in few-shot examples matter less than one might expect — swapping them for random labels often barely degrades performance, suggesting the examples primarily establish format rather than conveying label–input mappings. Important calibrating result for understanding what in-context learning actually does; directly relevant to the 'mechanistic account is open' caveat in the prose. §3–4 are the key sections.
